opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea in MrT5 is that we let the model learn for itself which tokens it can get rid of, rather than imposing some fixed rule from the outside. We start from ByT5, which operates directly on raw bytes, and that's great for robustness and for handling lots of languages, but the sequences get really long, which makes everything slow.

What we do is add what we call a delete gate. It's a small learned component that sits after a few of the early encoder layers. By that point, the model has had a chance to process the byte sequence and mix in some contextual information. The gate then outputs a score for each position that basically says whether this token should stay or be deleted. The tokens that get deleted are just removed from the sequence for the remaining layers, so everything downstream runs on a much shorter sequence.

The tricky part is that deletion is a discrete decision, and you can't directly backpropagate through "throw this token away." So during training we use a soft version of deletion. Instead of literally removing tokens, the gate values get added to the attention mask, so a token the model wants to delete gets effectively masked out in attention. That keeps everything differentiable. Then at inference time we do hard deletion and actually drop those tokens, which is where the speedups come from.

We also add a regularizer that encourages the model to delete more, and you can tune it to control how aggressive the compression is. One thing I find really interesting is that the model doesn't just learn arbitrary patterns. Because those first few layers have already done some contextual processing, the information from the deleted bytes gets merged into the tokens that remain. So you can think of it as the model learning its own dynamic tokenization, where it decides where the boundaries are. We see it doing things that look somewhat linguistically sensible, like deleting a lot within words and keeping certain positions around spaces or boundaries. It also adapts across languages, which is something a fixed tokenizer can't really do. And we can get pretty substantial reductions in sequence length with very little loss in performance on downstream tasks.

r001.rationale: It says early encoder layers add contextual information before the gate decides, and that information from deleted bytes is merged into the tokens that remain.

r002.rationale: It states that during training the gate values are added to the attention mask, effectively masking tokens the model wants to delete.

r003.rationale: It says inference uses hard deletion and actually drops selected tokens from the sequence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core idea with MrT5 is that we don't want to decide ahead of time, with some fixed rule, which bytes get dropped. We want the model to learn that itself. Byte-level models like ByT5 are great because you get rid of the tokenizer entirely, but the cost is that your sequences get really long, since every byte is its own token. So the question we were asking was: can the model figure out on its own which of those bytes are actually carrying information that needs to be propagated through the rest of the network, and which ones are redundant?

The way we do that is with a learned delete gate. After a few of the early encoder layers, we insert a gating mechanism that produces a score for each token, and that score determines whether the token gets kept or deleted before it moves on to the later layers. So the first few layers still see the full byte sequence, which gives the model a chance to do some contextualization, to sort of pool information from neighboring bytes into the representations that survive. Then at the gate, it can merge or compress that information and throw away the positions it no longer needs.

What's nice is that we don't tell it anything about linguistic structure. We don't say "drop whitespace" or "keep the first byte of every word." We just train it with a regularizer that encourages deletion, so there's pressure to shorten the sequence, and the model has to trade that off against actually solving the task. And what it ends up learning is really interesting. It often ends up deleting bytes in a way that looks a bit like a subword tokenizer, where it keeps, say, the end of a word or a chunk of characters that represents a unit, and it deletes the ones in between. But the key difference is that it's learned, it's contextual, and it's soft in the sense that the information from the deleted bytes isn't gone, it's been absorbed into the ones that remain.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that during training the gate is actually soft. We use a sigmoid-style gate and apply it through the attention mask, so the model can be trained end to end with gradients flowing through the deletion decisions. Then at inference time we make it hard, so we literally drop the tokens and get the real efficiency gains. That training-to-inference mismatch was something we had to think carefully about, but it works out pretty well in practice, and you can get something like fifty percent or more of the sequence deleted with very little loss in downstream performance.

r001.rationale: The response says early encoder layers contextualize the full byte sequence, pooling neighboring information into representations that survive before the gate drops tokens.

r002.rationale: It describes a learned gate trained end to end with soft scores applied through the attention mask, so the model learns deletion decisions during training.

r003.rationale: It states that at inference the gate becomes hard and tokens are literally dropped from the sequence.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that not every byte needs the same amount of computation. You start with a fine-grained input, but then you learn where you can compress it. In Mr. T5, a deletion gate looks at the contextual representations inside the encoder and assigns each token a score that determines whether it gets dropped. The remaining sequence is shorter, so the subsequent layers have less work to do.

And dropping a token at that point isn’t necessarily the same as deleting that character from the original text. There’s already been some contextual processing, so information from that token can be represented in neighboring tokens. The interesting question is whether the model can learn what to retain while still doing the task well, rather than us specifying fixed rules for what’s important.

r001.rationale: It says contextual processing happens before dropping and that information from a token can be represented in neighboring tokens.

r002.rationale: It describes a learned deletion gate but does not say tokens are masked out of attention during training.

r003.rationale: It says the remaining sequence is shorter, but does not state that selected tokens are physically deleted during inference.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to let the model learn which tokens it needs to keep, rather than specifying rules about which characters are important. We put a deletion gate partway through the encoder, and it makes a decision for each byte token based on its contextual representation. So by that point, the model has already had a chance to move information between neighboring tokens. Dropping a token doesn’t necessarily mean throwing away all the information associated with that byte.

Then we train with the language modeling objective alongside a loss that encourages deletion. Those objectives balance each other: we want the model to shorten the sequence, but still retain enough information to do the task well. So it’s really learning where it can compress the representation, rather than just identifying characters that are inherently unimportant.

r001.rationale: The response says the deletion gate acts on contextual representations after the encoder has had a chance to move information between neighboring tokens.

r002.rationale: It says the model learns which byte tokens to delete, but does not state that selected tokens are masked out of attention during training.

r003.rationale: It describes shortening the sequence, but does not state that selected tokens are physically deleted during inference.
